text_fidelity_a: Elgato Video Capture – USB 2.0 Capture Card Device, Easy to Use, Convert Analog to Digital, with VHS VCR TV to DVD Adapter, for Mac, Windows or iPad The reviews for these VHS converters were not impressive, but this one seemed to have an edge, so I took the chance. I'm glad I chose this one. It is working well. The instructions are not great, so you have to figure out how to get it to work. Lesson #1: save to a local hard drive. I store my video files on a large external (USB) drive, and when I had Elgato save directly to the external drive, I got errors and it wouldn't work. I thought the product was a dud. Then I switched to ripping to the local drive, and it works every time. Sometimes the audio and video are not in sync at first try, but has always worked the second try. It is also sensitive to your sound card drivers: if you try to use other audio applications (e.g. iTunes, Amazon Music, DAWs) while recording, the recording will be corrupted. So you either have to leave your computer alone while recording, or only use apps that don't use audio. The instructions don't tell you how to trim the video, but you can do that with the sliders; had to figure that one out on my own. Because of these little annoyances, I only gave it 4 stars.

text_fidelity_a:
Audio-Technica ATH-LS50iSBK In-Ear Monitor Headphones with In-Line Mic & Control, Black These headphones fall between ones I currently own and are, I'd say, a fair price to pay.

In terms of listening to music, they easily out perform standard come-with or cheap earbuds, no doubt about that. So if you're looking to upgrade from that sort and you don't mind the money, it's a no-brainer. They were a bit better than my next step up earphones--more full, more rich, with better base. They fell a little short of my Jaybirds. Again, these have a nice rich sound, but the Jaybirds were crisper, the Audio-Technica ones a bit more muddy.

The fit is excellent. These are very comfortable, the over-the-ear both stable and comfortable--you don't notice it once you're wearing them and they stayed in place nicely while running. They come with a medium size fit, but also come with two smaller sizes.

The microphone worked quite well, people had no trouble hearing or understanding me. I would have liked the control to be adjustable, or a little lower down, but I get why it isn't. Just a personal preference.

So in the end, these seem well priced. They're more expensive than some, but in comparison to those I own that are cheaper than these, the Audio-Technica out-performs them. They don't sound as good as my Jaybirds, but then, they also cost a good amount less, so I wouldn't expect anything different.

In the end, it's you get what you pay for and so it's all up to whether you like to pay for better sound, fit, and comfort. I'm obviously a yes, so I'd say these are worth picking up to replace you're cheaper set.
text_fidelity_b: Audio-Technica ATH-LS50iSBK In-Ear Monitor Headphones with In-Line Mic & Control, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Case Logic BEBP-115 15.6-Inch Laptop and Tablet Backpack, Black First a caveat: I am not of the generation who grew up carrying backpacks to school and I do not have a lot of shoulder/upper arm strength; in addition I have arthritis in my neck, so to me any backpack seems a bit strange, stiff, and awkward. Frankly, I think if I'd had to carry around all the books I did in junior high school in a backpack (none of my classes were near my homeroom locker, so there was none of this dropping books off routine--we only had three minutes to get between classes), I'd have severe back problems right now, remembering the thick English, math, science, Italian, and history textbooks, plus a full size ring binder. Oy.

Now to our backpack: I like this. We have less expensive backpacks in our home, to use as a "bug out" bag in case of emergency. This is much nicer: padding, quality of material, and lots of nice pockets (I am a pockets-type person). I particularly like the "hidden pocket" that faces your back, which would be useful for money or any other valuables if you were backpacking or traveling. I have preliminarily tested this by putting my laptop and my 10-inch tablet in the space provided and walking around for a bit. My laptop is six years old and weighs a ton. However, the padded shoulder straps and the sternum strap were helpful in keeping this balanced well on my back. I went up and down stairs a few times and did not feel unbalanced or "top heavy." (I do now, however, understand why people like Airbooks.)

In addition to the laptop pocket with the inner sleeve for the tablet, this has a central compartment with two pockets, one zipped, and an outside compartment with all sorts of slots for pens, memory cards, CDs, whatever. A small pocket on the top of the back could hold a cell phone or perhaps your printout of a boarding pass, parking ticket receipt, whatever, and there are two small pockets, one on each side, one with an opening so you could put an .mp3 player in the pocket and have your earbuds come out through it. This is all in addition to the "hidden pocket." There is a strong handle at either end of the backpack as well as a handle.

My goal is to give this a better workout at Dragoncon, where I can carry lunch and snacks and juice boxes in the central compartment, carry my tablet in the laptop compartment, and also carry my camera, instead of slinging a lunchbox and my camera case over my shoulder. It seems like a much better option. I also see it being useful on the occasional weekend trip. If it works out for me, it's possible my husband might enjoy one as well.

[September: This was really, really good at Dragoncon; I will be using a backpack again next year. Much better than carrying the lunchbox and the camera separately and wearing a pouch. I put my tablet in the laptop pocket, my lunch things (juice boxes, sandwiches, snacks, fruit) in the middle pocket, and the camera in the outermost pocket. The little pocket at the top held my spare cell phone batteries, and my wallet was in the hidden pocket. This backpack needs a strap at the bottom, and, instead of an iPod holder, a water bottle holder. That's the only thing I can see wrong with it. Yeah, I could have put a water bottle inside with my lunch.]

[PS I liked this so much I bought my husband one for Christmas.]
text_fidelity_b: Case Logic BEBP-115 15.6-Inch Laptop and Tablet Backpack, Black

text_fidelity_a:
BRAINWAVZ Cradle Headphone Hanger, Universal Stand for Sennheiser, Sony, Bose, Beats, AKG, Audio-Technica, Gaming Controller, Cables, Gamepad & Other Gaming Accessories (Peridot) Shortly after I received this as a review sample it quickly became a permanent part of my home studio. Right now my [[ASIN:B00ENZRS76 Brainwavz HM9 Hi-Fi Noise Isolating Headphones]] are mounted for immediate use, and I tested this with some smaller phones I also use like the [[ASIN:B0002F74E8 Sony MDR7502 Professional Stereo Headphone]] and they fit perfectly as well.

This is a tall, thin stand that measures ten inches tall with a relatively short five inch base. Despite the proportions this sits stably and is not apt to tip if you accidentally bump into it. I love the contoured top over which the phones rest. That holds the phones in a natural shape. For expensive phones that is not especially a problem because the over the head mechanisms on those devices are usually very well made.

The material (I am guessing plexi-glass) is 8mm thick (about a third of an inch), and is flexible. Complaints about the large logo are valid if you want a cleaner look, but since I am currently using Brainwavz headphones - and this is in my music studio - the aesthetics are a non-issue for me. I care more about function and convenient storage and this stand provides both of those.

For me the convenience of having my phones readily available is important because I use them often. This stand is an inexpensive way of accomplishing that.

Jabra Stealth Bluetooth Headset - Black (US Version) I am pleased with this headset; the sound quality is good and audibility is very sharp. The music quality is also good. Assembly is very simple and needs no additional tools to set it together. It also fits well into my ears. I have been using this set for the last three weeks and it works great. It is paired with my cell phone and I use this to listen to the incoming calls and also listen to the music from micro SD card inserted into the cell phone. It is small and has a discreet design. It is very light, easy to carry and works great. The gadget also synchronizes easily with phone, but it does not pair with my Garmin Nuvi GPS machine or my Acer Chromebook both of which are Bluetooth-enabled.

Pairing with cell phone is very easy; just turn the headset on and the cell phone on, it detects the Bluetooth easily and within a minute it gives the message that it is paired. The built-in battery is excellent, and on one charge it lasts for about 5-6 hours of use time. The downside is that this piece doesn't have a separate mute button or the volume button; you have to control volume from your cell phone. Another negative feature is that the three replacement parts for earpiece that comes with the set are of same size, hence gives little option for someone with small (or large) ears. text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Galaxy NX EK-GN120ZKAXAR Galaxy Wireless Smart Android 4G Camera 20.3MP Mirrorless Digital Camera with 4.8-Inch LCD with 18-55mm OIS Lens (Black) My first impression upon unboxing this camera was "Wow, that feels cheap." Everything's made from unattractive plastic. The single dial on the top rear of the camera (oddly blank) feels light, spins too easily and clicking it feels mushy. The other buttons on the camera, power, movie and flash all have the same, cheap, mushy feel. The shutter button has poor tactile feel.

The camera is surprisingly heavy; for me uncomfortably, painfully, so.The back is so taken up by the huge 4.8" LCD screen that the thumb rest is too short, more of an afterthought that cause me quite a bit of discomfort during extended use. The DSLR style handgrip is quite large (perhaps too large for small hands) to accommodate the massive 4360 mAh battery.

On paper the idea of an Android OS with a 4.8" LCD screen and a big APS-C sensor sounds great but I was sadly less than impressed.

Because of the Android OS startup time from fully off to ready to shoot is a very long 23 seconds. In standby mode the camera was ready to shoot in approx. 4 seconds. The camera runs warm, very warm, even just sitting idle on a cool 50 degree day. I would worry about overheating in the summer months.

Image quality was unimpressive especially in low light. Early morning, post sunrise, images with sky and clouds were extremely grainy and noisy. Performance in full light was better but not spectacular. Auto focus was run of the mill, often seeking excessively in low light situations. High ISO performance was exceedingly poor. Past ISO 800 images were rather noisier and grainy. In auto mode the camera seemed to make poor choices for ISO and shutter speeds.

Controls. Almost every setting is accessed via the large LCD screen.

There are over twenty pre-configured shooting modes. I used several of them while checking out this camera. These selections are made from a top to bottom scrolling 'carousel' where you scroll through until you find the option you want. I found it annoying to find and stop on the mode I wanted. You're going to miss shots trying to find the mode you want.

Continuous Shooting: burst mode. Surprisingly fast.
Kids Shot: the camera plays one of three sounds to attract a child's attention and then bursts five photos.
Macro: The Galaxy NX has a surprisingly short minimum focal distance with the kit lens and the macro photos I took were among the best results I was able to get from the camera.
Rich Tone: Samsung's HDR mode. Processing time was excessive.
Panorama: This is a sweep mode, smoothly move the camera (a tripod helps) to capture up to 180°'s of view. Disappointingly the camera reduces the image size significantly in Panorama mode.
Multi Exposure: combines two or more images into one.
Drama: combines several images of a moving subject into a single image. The camera was very picky about detecting moving objects. I encountered at least a 50% fail rate trying this mode. Additionally, as with the Panorama mode the image size is greatly reduced.

The camera can also be used in manual mode. Samsung calls it 'Expert Mode'. This gives you access to the standard PASM controls. The settings are controlled by three half-circle on screen dials that I found frustratingly hard to use. Try to change one and my thick fingers would spin the wrong dial. Using Shutter Priority mode I found the processing time of 30 second exposures was a disappointing additional 30 seconds.

There are some things I did like about this camera. It's not all bad. It can produce decent images and I honestly think the majority of the limitations I experienced were due to the cheap kit lens. The 4.8" LCD is gorgeous, in the right light, I recently went back to a camera with a beautiful 3" screen and it felt small. Some of the included shooting modes are fun to play with. Connectivity via WiFi was rock solid (I wasn't able to test the 3G/4G connectivity) even in parking lots of places that offered free WiFi. There were eleven gigs of free space in internal memory. That was plenty of room for a day's shooting and testing. I never did get around to installing an SD card.

In conclusion...
I'm not really sure who this camera is aimed at. They seem to be trying to attract smart phone users with the ability to access the internet almost anywhere and instantly share you photos. But do you really need an expensive, heavy and complex large-sensor camera to post photos to Facebook and Twitter?
On the flip side I just can't see this camera being attractive to professional photographers or high end photography enthusiasts. While the inclusion of the electronic viewfinder is nice I found the all on-screen controls to be distracting and bothersome and the image quality was for the most part lackluster.

A note about durability. As I was finishing up the testing of this camera I bobbled the camera due to nerve damage and it took a spill. The height was not great, less than three feet, and the initial impact was on soil and grass. The lens came apart into numerous pieces. I was able to put the lens back together but it appears to have suffered internal damage and will not focus either automatically or manually. I accept that I caused this damage but I am very unimpressed with the durability of such an expensive camera.

I really can't recommend this camera. Three stars but barely.

A side note about Samsung's technical support that isn't reflected in my rating of this camera. Calling Samsung's support line was a complete nightmare. Audio quality was atrocious. At the end I was practically screaming to be heard. I spent close to an hour and a half on the phone speaking with seven different people. Each person I spoke to had to be told all my information, the camera's information and the reason for my call. Four times I was transferred to 'the proper department.' In the end I had a supervisor tell me, first that the camera did not exist and then, that it must be a UK version and I'd have to start all over and call their UK support line. I then contacted Samsung through their Facebook support page. It's been almost a week and they still haven't decided what to do about the camera/lens.

{Edit}
It took nearly a month of back and forth and arguing to get Samsung to agree my camera was a US version, it was under warranty and they would issue a repair ticket for it. It was shipped off at their expense, repaired surprisingly quickly and shipped back. The camera's now in working order. Only one thing marred the process. When they returned the camera and lens the put a cap on the rear of the lens (I'd shipped it with the lens attached) but only put a piece of what looked like a Post-It across the body opening. I found it odd they wouldn't properly cap the body to protect the sensor though on the whole the packing job, bubble wrapped and foam peanuts was well done. Kudos to their repair facility but I'm still very put off by the whole experience with their support people.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Galaxy NX EK-GN120ZKAXAR Galaxy Wireless Smart Android 4G Camera 20.3MP Mirrorless Digital Camera with 4.8-Inch LCD with 18-55mm OIS Lens (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Fire TV Stick 4K, brilliant 4K streaming quality, TV and smart home controls, free and live TV I’ve had a few Fire TV sticks over the years, and generally I love them. For this model, the first one I got was a dud. It died in 2 days. Amazon took me through some reasonable troubleshooting steps, then replaced it quickly and easily. The second one is a lot better.

In general, I find the remote has a weird tendency to, I guess “rot” is the word. The case starts to feel like it’s covered in a sticky mess. I don’t know why. I guess that’s why the remote covers are so popular. Not a stopping point – they still work – just a point of note. The optional game controllers do not have this issue.

There are ample streaming options. I’ve yet to look for something, even less common things like Wonderium and Funimation, and not find it. The UI is easy to navigate. The device is responsive. I put it through a 7.1 sound system and it can handle that no problem.

A few things to note, not exactly faults of the product, but faults you will encounter while using the product.

For the Disney+ login, the trick of using the phone just errors out and asks to re-authenticate over and over. If you use a strong password, that can be a pain. Once it works, it’s fine, just a pain to set up.

For the Ubisoft+ integration, for many of the games it starts to load then fails. I don’t see the same issue on the same games on PC, so it’s probably related to the app. This was the primary purpose for which I bought the device, so it is a bit of a disappointment. Also note, you need the Luna service for this, which is totally worth it on its own, by the way. Also, at least for me, while the video streaming was fine over WiFi, the gaming required the Ethernet adapter.

It’s not perfect, but it’s outstanding for such a low price. I often use it rather than power up my PS5 to watch Netflix because it is so much more convenient, and of identical quality.
text_fidelity_b: Fire TV Stick 4K, brilliant 4K streaming quality, TV and smart home controls, free and live TV

SAMSUNG 55-Inch Class QLED Q60B Series - 4K UHD Dual LED Quantum HDR Smart TV with Alexa Built-in (QN55Q60BAFXZA, 2022 Model) So...

I bought the 43" QLED Q60B. Also bought the Samsung 9200S soundbar with wireless sub, and then bought their wireless rear speakers. That part is awesome, but will be a separate review.

1- Despite checking answers and even asking the Samsung Specialist about Hands Free Alexa (ie. don't press the MIC button), the 2022 version DOES NOT have this feature, which of course, after buying it, installing it 10ft up in the corner of the bedroom, and trying to make it work.... had to call Samsung directly to troubleshoot, who said it is not available after 2021. Even Bixby, which I can't stand, is grayed out.

2- Not-so-Smart. I have had a ROKU on all my other Samsung TVs because they were older. So I became accustomed to much more variety it seems. Other than the big ones, the variety is disappointing, even in the music section.

3- I do not buy a TV outright only to have the manufacturer decide what I CAN'T remove. The first damn option in your "customizing" short cut bar, is SAMSUNG'S forced-on-you advertising slot, that cannot be moved out of the or removed, and I have no interest in it! There are a few others that can't be dropped, but can be moved.

4- Despite trying to follow the trend to smaller remotes, they missed the mark. People want quick access to things. Mute should ALWAYS have it's own button, not remembering to press and hold a specific button to mute it. Your Settings access is NOT intuitive. I trying to make it easier, you somehow over-complicated it. Some items are ambiguous (maybe it's under this one?), and I find myself searching for things and when I finally find them, the controls are often limited.

It's 2022, I just bought a quality TV from a previously adored and promoted-by-me brand, and I'm super pissed. My buddy's LG is much better, and I'm now going to add a fricking Roku to a TV that is state of the art. And for a 43" I could have gotten an off-name brand with awesome pic and Roku built in, for half the price!!!! Lesson Learned!

Boo to Samsung on this. And don't send me to your useless Facebook help page when you already dropped the ball!
text_fidelity_b: SAMSUNG 55-Inch Class QLED Q60B Series - 4K UHD Dual LED Quantum HDR Smart TV with Alexa Built-in (QN55Q60BAFXZA, 2022 Model)

NuForce Optoma BE2 Wireless Bluetooth Earphones with Patented SpinFit eartips, 10h Battery, Microphone, AAC Support for iPhone I rarely use ear bud type earphones because they always hurt my ears. I prefer traditional over the ear, cushioned earphones as a rule. However, there are times when the extra bulk is a problem - like on horseback.

These have a couple of different size ear pieces and I have been able to get the fit adjusted enough to wear them comfortably for a couple of hours straight. The sound is good with classical music and country. I don't do the whole extra bass type of thing, so I cannot comment on that aspect. I can clearly hear the French horns, clarinets and background piano in several different pieces of music.

My issue here is that these don't connect by Bluetooth easily to every device. It took multiple tries to connect to my LG V10 phone, they never connected with my husband's Sony Xperia phone or my Android tablet, but they did connect to my Samsung tablet after two tries. These devices are all current and have updated software.
